topics.title: --force
topics.description: `--force` (or `-f`) allows commands unless they are explicitly denied, and in print mode it lets the agent apply file changes. `--yolo` is an alias. Use it only in environments you trust, because the agent will not stop to ask.

topics.title: --help
topics.description: `--help` (or `-h`) prints the commands and options available in your installed version. It is the most reliable reference because the CLI changes between releases. Add it after a subcommand, such as `agent mcp --help`, to see that command's options.

topics.title: --mode
topics.description: `--mode` sets the starting mode to `plan` or `ask`. Agent mode is the default when the flag is not used. Plan mode designs an approach first, and Ask mode is read-only. `--plan` is a shorthand for `--mode=plan`.

topics.title: --model
topics.description: `--model` selects the model for one run. Use `agent models` to see valid IDs. Inside a session, `/model` changes it without restarting.

topics.title: --output-format
topics.description: `--output-format` chooses how print mode formats its result: `text`, `json` or `stream-json`. `text` gives the final answer only, `json` gives structured output and `stream-json` emits progress events as they happen. It requires `--print`.

topics.title: --print
topics.description: `--print` (or `-p`) runs the agent non-interactively and prints the response, with access to all tools. Use it in scripts and CI. File edits are only proposed unless you also pass `--force`. In scripts, `--trust` skips the workspace trust prompt and `--approve-mcps` approves MCP servers automatically, so use both only on projects you control.

topics.title: --resume
topics.description: `--resume [chatId]` resumes a chat session. With a chat ID it loads that thread, and without one it opens a picker. `--continue` is an alias that picks up the previous session, and `agent ls` shows chat IDs.

topics.title: --sandbox
topics.description: `--sandbox` sets the sandbox mode to `enabled` or `disabled`. When enabled, commands run with limited file and network access. The setting persists, and `/sandbox` changes it inside a session.

topics.title: --version
topics.description: `--version` (or `-v`) prints the installed Cursor CLI version. Run `agent --version` after installing to confirm that the install worked. The CLI updates itself by default, and `agent update` updates it manually.

topics.title: --workspace
topics.description: `--workspace` sets the working directory the agent uses. It lets you start the CLI on a project without changing folders in your shell. The directory becomes the workspace for file access.

topics.title: --worktree
topics.description: `--worktree` (or `-w`) runs the agent in a new Git worktree, with a generated name if you give none. Use `--worktree-base` to base it on a branch and `--skip-worktree-setup` to skip the setup scripts in `.cursor/worktrees.json`. Your main checkout stays untouched.

Typing `@` opens a picker to add files, folders, terminal output, past chats, Git diffs or the browser to your prompt. The agent then reads exactly what you pointed to. In the CLI it works for files and folders.

topics.title: Advanced Features
topics.description: Advanced features go beyond chat and code edits. The Browser tool lets the agent test your running app, Canvas shows results as interactive views, Voice Chat lets you talk to the agent, and `/goal` keeps it working on a long task until it is done.

topics.title: Agent Modes
topics.description: Agent modes set how much the agent is allowed to do. Agent has full tool access, Ask is read-only, Plan researches the code and writes a plan before any change, Debug collects runtime evidence to find a root cause, and Design lets you annotate your running app. You switch modes with `Shift+Tab` or the mode picker.
resources: Cursor Modes Explained: Agent, Ask, Plan, and Debug

topics.title: Agent Security
topics.description: Agents can act in unexpected ways because of prompt injection or model mistakes, so Cursor puts guardrails around what they can do. Sensitive actions need your approval by default, including terminal commands, MCP connections and each MCP tool call unless you allowlist it. Reading files and searching code need no approval, while edits to config files do, and other edits are saved right away, so keep your work in version control. Network access from the agent's tools is limited by default to GitHub, direct link retrieval and web search providers.

topics.title: Agent Window
topics.description: The Agents Window is an agent-first interface for working with many agents across repositories and environments, including local, cloud and remote SSH. It adds a diffs view for reviewing, committing and managing pull requests, and it supports worktrees and handing tasks between local and cloud. Open it with `Open Agents Window` in the Command Palette, and return to the classic editor with `Open IDE`.
resources: Cursor Agents Window: Multi-Agent UI, Cloud Runs & PR Handoff
Setting Up the NEW Cursor Agent Window

topics.title: agent
topics.description: `agent` starts the Cursor CLI in interactive mode. You can pass a starting prompt, for example `agent "explain this project"`. It opens in Agent mode by default, and you can switch modes with `Shift+Tab`. Run it from the root of your project, or set another folder with `--workspace`.

topics.title: Agent
topics.description: Agent is the default mode, with full access to tools: searching files, reading and editing code, running shell commands and using the browser. It is meant for complex tasks that need many steps. Which actions need your approval depends on your run mode.

topics.title: AGENTS.md
topics.description: `AGENTS.md` is a plain markdown instruction file with no metadata. Cursor reads it from the project root and from subdirectories, and nested files combine with their parents so the most specific instructions win. It is a simple choice when you want one file that other coding tools can read too.
resources: Does Cursor read AGENTS.md, and should you use it or Cursor rules?
How to Create AGENTS.md in Cursor AI (2026)

topics.title: /ask
topics.description: `/ask` toggles Ask mode for read-only questions. In this mode the agent can read and search but does not change files. Use it to explore code safely.

topics.title: Ask
topics.description: Ask mode is for read-only questions. The agent searches and reads your code and answers, but it does not edit files or run commands that change anything. Use it to learn a codebase or to think through an idea safely.

topics.title: Auto & Cursor Router
topics.description: Auto lets Cursor choose the model for you. Cost mode favors lower token spend, while Balance and Intelligence use Cursor Router, which classifies each request by task type and difficulty and sends it to a suitable model. Cursor Router is available on Teams and Enterprise plans, and individual plans use Cost mode.

topics.title: Automation
topics.description: Automation runs Cursor without you at the keyboard. Headless mode runs the agent from scripts and CI, GitHub Actions can call it in a workflow, Automations start Cloud Agents on a schedule or when an event happens, and Bugbot reviews pull requests for you.

topics.title: Browser Tool
topics.description: The Browser tool lets the agent control a web view inside Cursor. It can open pages, click, type, scroll, take screenshots and read console and network output, so it can test your app or check a visual change. State is kept per workspace, and tool use needs approval by default.
resources: Run End-to-End Tests from Your Terminal with Kane CLI
NEW Cursor 2.0 Browser: SHOW to AI Agent What You Mean

topics.title: Bugbot
topics.description: Bugbot is an automated pull request reviewer that looks for bugs, security issues and quality problems and leaves comments with fix suggestions. It runs on each PR update, or when you comment `cursor review` or `bugbot run`. Autofix can start a Cloud Agent to fix the findings, and you can add project guidance in `.cursor/BUGBOT.md`.
resources: AI Code Reviews in Cursor (BugBot Tutorial)

topics.title: Canvas
topics.description: Canvases are interactive views that open next to the chat, such as dashboards, audits and reports with sections, stats and tables. Cursor creates one when a visual format suits the task, or when you ask for one. You can refresh it with new data and publish a read-only snapshot link to teammates on paid team plans.
resources: Cursor Canvas Guide: What It Is and What to Build With It
How to Use Cursor as a Designer

topics.title: Choosing Models
topics.description: The model picker in the agent panel lets you choose between Cursor's own models and models from providers such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Google. In the CLI, use `/model`, `--model` or `agent models` to see what is available. Pick a faster model for simple edits and a stronger one for hard reasoning.
resources: Cursor model selection — there is a guide you can follow that actually helps

topics.title: /clear
topics.description: `/clear` starts a new chat session, and `/new`, `/new-chat` and `/newchat` are aliases. Use it when you move to an unrelated task, so old context does not get in the way. Your previous chat can be reopened with `/resume`.

topics.title: CLI
topics.description: Cursor CLI brings the same agent to the terminal on macOS, Linux and Windows. You install it with a one-line script, start it with `agent`, work interactively with Agent, Plan and Ask modes, or run one-off prompts with `-p` in scripts and CI. It reads the same rules and MCP configuration as the editor.
resources: Getting Started with Cursor CLI: A Complete Guide
Cursor CLI Tutorial for Beginners (should you use it?)

topics.title: Cloud Agents
topics.description: Cloud Agents run in isolated cloud VMs with a full development environment, so they keep working when your laptop is closed. Each agent clones your repository, works on its own branch, tests what it builds and opens a pull request with artifacts such as screenshots and logs. You can run many in parallel and start them from the editor, web, mobile, Slack, GitHub, Linear or the API. They were previously called Background Agents.
resources: Cursor cloud agents and automations: what to automate first
How To Use Cursor Agents For Beginners

topics.title: Cmd+/
topics.description: `Cmd+/` (`Ctrl+/` on Windows and Linux) loops between AI models. It lets you quickly change the model for the next message. Use the model picker when you want to see the full list.

topics.title: Cmd+Enter
topics.description: `Cmd+Enter` sends your message immediately and skips the queue while the agent is busy. When the agent has suggested changes to review, the same keys accept all of them. Plain `Enter` queues the message instead, and pressing it again or using `Send now` steers the agent at its next tool call.

topics.title: Cmd+I
topics.description: `Cmd+I` (`Ctrl+I` on Windows and Linux) opens the Agent in the side panel. `Cmd+L` and `Cmd+K` also toggle the side panel. It is the fastest way to start a prompt from the editor.

topics.title: Cmd+N
topics.description: `Cmd+N` starts a new chat, and `Cmd+R` does the same. Starting a fresh chat for each task keeps the context clean. `Cmd+T` opens a new chat tab, and `Cmd+[` and `Cmd+]` move between chats.

topics.title: Cmd+Shift+Backspace
topics.description: `Cmd+Shift+Backspace` cancels the agent's current generation. When there are suggested changes to review, the same keys reject all of them, and `Cmd+Enter` accepts all of them. Use it to stop the agent quickly when it goes in the wrong direction.

topics.title: Cmd+Shift+L
topics.description: `Cmd+Shift+L` adds the code you selected in the editor to the chat as context. It gives the agent the exact lines you mean without copying and pasting. `Cmd+K` or `Cmd+L` with a selection adds it to a new chat instead.

topics.title: Cmd+Shift+P
topics.description: `Cmd+Shift+P` opens the Command Palette, which lists the commands that Cursor and your extensions provide. It is where you run `Open Agents Window` and `Open IDE`, and where you find Keyboard Shortcuts to see or change any key binding.

topics.title: Cursor Models
topics.description: Cursor Models are the models Cursor offers itself: Composer 2.5 and the Grok 4.7, 4.6 and 4.5 family. They draw from the weekly pool included with paid plans, and the Plus plan can use only these models. Third-party models from other providers are billed separately.

topics.title: Composer
topics.description: Composer is Cursor's own agentic model family. The current version, Composer 2.5, is tuned for long tasks, tool use, file edits and terminal work inside Cursor. It draws from your plan's usage pool for Cursor models, and the faster variant is the default for interactive sessions at a higher price per token.

topics.title: /config
topics.description: `/config` opens an interactive menu for CLI settings. Changes are saved in `cli-config.json`, so they persist between sessions. It is an easy way to change options without editing JSON.

topics.title: Cursor Models
topics.description: Cursor Models are the models Cursor offers itself: Composer ans Grok. They draw from the weekly pool included with paid plans, and the Plus plan can use only these models. Third-party models from other providers are billed separately.

topics.title: Cursor Router
topics.description: Auto lets Cursor choose the model for you. Cost mode favors lower token spend, while Balance and Intelligence use Cursor Router, which classifies each request by task type and difficulty and sends it to a suitable model. Cursor Router is available on Teams and Enterprise plans, and individual plans use Cost mode.
resources: Cursor Router: How Auto Picks a Model for Every Request
I Tested Cursor Router So You Don't Have To

topics.title: Cursor SDK
topics.description: The Cursor SDK lets you run the same agent from your own code. The TypeScript package `@cursor/sdk` and a Python SDK create an agent with `Agent.create()`, send it prompts and stream the events. You choose a local runtime that works on files in your machine, or a cloud runtime that runs in a Cursor-hosted VM.
resources: What the Cursor SDK is for, and when an automation is enough
I tested Cursor's Agents SDK, and it blew my mind

topics.title: Cursor Tab
topics.description: Cursor Tab is AI autocomplete that suggests code from your recent edits, nearby code and linter errors. Press `Tab` to accept a suggestion, or `Cmd+Right Arrow` to accept one word at a time, and press `Tab` again to jump to the next predicted edit. It can change several lines and edit other files, and you can snooze it or turn it off for chosen file types.
resources: Meet Cursor Tab and Never Look Back: The Future of AI-Assisted Coding
Cursor Tab: How Autocomplete Predicts Your Next Edit

topics.title: Cursor vs Claude vs Codex
topics.description: Cursor, Claude Code and Codex are all coding agents that read a repository, edit files and run commands, but they come from different places. Cursor is an editor-first product that lets you choose models from several providers, including its own Composer models. Claude Code is Anthropic's agent for Claude models, and Codex is OpenAI's agent for OpenAI models. The three share many conventions, so Cursor can load `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, and skills and subagents stored in the `.claude` and `.codex` folders.
resources: Codex vs Cursor Review: Which AI Coding Tool Actually Wins?

topics.title: Customization
topics.description: Customization lets you adapt Cursor to your project and your team. Rules and `AGENTS.md` hold standing instructions, skills package repeatable tasks, MCP connects external tools, plugins bundle these together, and hooks run your own scripts during the agent loop.

topics.title: Debug
topics.description: Debug Mode finds root causes by collecting runtime evidence before changing code. The agent proposes hypotheses, adds log statements, asks you to reproduce the bug, reads the logs, applies a small fix and then cleans up the instrumentation. Use it for bugs where guessing from the code alone does not work.
resources: Introducing Debug Mode: Agents with runtime logs
Cursor's Debug Mode Is Arguably Its Best Feature
Debug Mode Fixed My Bugs Automatically (Multi-Agent Features)

topics.title: /debug
topics.description: `/debug` toggles Debug mode, or runs a prompt in Debug mode when you add text. The agent collects runtime evidence before it changes code. It suits bugs that need real logs to understand.

topics.title: Design
topics.description: Design Mode lets you leave notes on your running app inside the browser of the Agents Window. You click an element, an area or text, describe the change, and the agent edits the code. Each note carries element details and a screenshot, so the agent knows exactly what you mean. Toggle it with `Cmd+Shift+D`.
resources: Direct agents with visual prompts in Design Mode
Design 10X Faster with the NEW Cursor Design Mode

topics.title: Desktop
topics.description: The desktop editor is the classic Cursor experience: code editor, Agent side panel, Tab autocomplete and diff review in one window. Use it when you want to read and edit code while the agent works. It runs on macOS, Windows and Linux. Extensions come from the Open VSX registry, so a few VS Code extensions may be missing or behave differently.
resources: The VS Code/Cursor Setup to INCREASE Productivity (2025)

topics.title: Everyday Workflows
topics.description: Everyday workflows are the repeatable ways you work with the agent. You explore a codebase, write clear prompts, plan before larger changes, edit and test, fix bugs and review the diffs. Starting with questions and plans before edits keeps each change small and easy to review.

topics.title: Explore Codebases
topics.description: Ask the agent to explain how a project is organized, where a feature lives or how a request flows through the code. It searches files and folders, reads the relevant ones and answers with references. Ask mode is a good fit because it is read-only and makes no changes.
resources: How AI Cursor Coding Agent Actually Explore Your Codebase: An End-to-End Look at Context Gathering

topics.title: Fix Bugs & Refactoring
topics.description: Give the agent the error message, the steps to reproduce and the expected behavior. For bugs that are hard to explain, Debug Mode adds logging, asks you to reproduce the problem and finds the cause from real runtime data. The agent then makes a targeted fix and removes the logging. For refactoring, describe the change you want and ask the agent to run your tests afterwards to confirm that behavior did not change.
resources: Coding agents for the hardest bugs

topics.title: /fork
topics.description: `/fork` copies the current chat into a new session. The original stays unchanged, so you can explore another approach and still return. It is useful before a risky or experimental change.

topics.title: Forking
topics.description: Forking copies the current conversation into a new session so you can try a different approach without losing the original. In the CLI, use `/fork`. Chats can also be moved between local and cloud in the Agents Window.

topics.title: Git Worktrees
topics.description: A Git worktree is a separate checkout of the same repository, so each agent task gets its own files and your main checkout stays untouched. In the Agents Window worktrees are built in, and in the editor you use `/worktree`. A `.cursor/worktrees.json` file defines setup steps such as installing dependencies and copying `.env` files.
resources: Devs can no longer avoid learning Git worktree
How I Use Worktrees with Codex and Cursor

topics.title: GitHub Actions
topics.description: You can run Cursor CLI inside a GitHub Actions workflow to review code, fix lint errors or update docs automatically. The workflow installs the CLI, adds it to the path and runs `agent -p` with `CURSOR_API_KEY` stored as a repository secret. Restricted autonomy, where CI handles commits and pushes, is recommended for production.

topics.title: /goal
topics.description: `/goal` gives the agent a long-lived objective to work on until it is fully complete. You write the objective after the command, and you can pause with `Ctrl+C`. The feature is rolling out gradually.

topics.title: Grok
topics.description: Grok is a model family that Cursor offers as one of its own models, with Grok 4.7, 4.6 and 4.5 available. Each has Fast variants that respond quicker at a higher price. Because they are Cursor models, they draw from your plan's weekly pool instead of prepaid credit.
resources: I Spent 50 Hours Using Grok 4.7 (here is its best use case)

topics.title: Headless Mode
topics.description: Headless mode runs the agent without the interactive interface, using `agent -p "prompt"` (the `--print` flag). By default changes are only proposed, so add `--force` to let it edit files. You choose `text`, `json` or `stream-json` output with `--output-format`, which makes results easy to use in scripts.

topics.title: /help
topics.description: `/help` shows the available slash commands, and `/help <command>` shows details for one. Commands change between versions, so this is the best way to see what your CLI supports.

topics.title: Hooks
topics.description: Hooks are scripts that observe, control or extend the agent loop. You define them in `.cursor/hooks.json` for events such as `preToolUse`, `beforeShellExecution`, `afterFileEdit` and `stop`. A hook receives JSON on stdin and returns JSON on stdout, and exit code 2 blocks the action. Teams use them for formatting, audit logs and custom approval rules.
resources: Deep Dive into the new Cursor Hooks

topics.title: Ignore Files
topics.description: A `.cursorignore` file in the project root lists files and folders that Cursor should keep out of AI context. Cursor already skips `.env` files, `.git/` and lock files, and it respects `.gitignore`. Ignored files are blocked from the agent, but terminal commands and MCP tools run outside these controls and may still read them.
resources: Cursor Ignore File (.cursorignore): Syntax, Setup and Context Optimization

topics.title: Integrations
topics.description: Integrations connect Cursor to the tools where your team already works. You can hand tasks to Cloud Agents from Slack, Linear or Jira, and get pull request reviews and agent work on GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket and Azure DevOps. Most integrations are set up by an admin from the Cursor dashboard.

topics.title: Introduction
topics.description: Cursor is an AI code editor built around a coding agent. The agent searches your repository, reads files, edits code, runs terminal commands and reports what it changed. You can use it in the desktop editor, in a separate Agents Window, from the terminal with the Cursor CLI, in the cloud, and from your phone. These surfaces share the same agent, rules and MCP configuration.
resources: Cursor Crash Course & AI Coding For Beginners

topics.title: login
topics.description: `agent login` opens your default browser so you can sign in to Cursor, and stores the credentials locally. If the browser does not open, run `NO_OPEN_BROWSER=1 agent login` to print the URL. For scripts and CI, set the `CURSOR_API_KEY` environment variable or pass `--api-key` instead. Your login is stored locally until you log out.

topics.title: logout
topics.description: `agent logout` signs you out and clears the stored authentication. Use it on shared machines or when you want to switch accounts. The next `agent` run will ask you to sign in again.

topics.title: /logs
topics.description: `/logs` shows the path of the CLI debug log and copies it to the clipboard. Attach that file when you report a problem or when you need to see what the CLI did. `/copy-request-id` copies the ID of the last request, which support can use too.

topics.title: ls
topics.description: `agent ls` shows your previous chats and lets you pick one to resume. It is the quickest way to return to work from an earlier session. For the most recent chat, `agent resume` is shorter.

topics.title: Manage Context
topics.description: Long conversations fill the model's context window and can lower the quality of answers. Run `/summarize` (alias `/compress`) to condense the conversation, start a new chat for each new task, and use `@` mentions to add only what the task needs. Side chats keep tangents out of the main thread.
resources: Cursor Context Management: Rules, AGENTS.md, and MCP

topics.title: mcp
topics.description: `agent mcp` manages MCP servers from the terminal. The subcommands `list`, `list-tools`, `login`, `enable` and `disable` show server status, show a server's tools, sign in to OAuth servers and control which servers are approved. The CLI reads the same `mcp.json` as the editor.

topics.title: /mcp
topics.description: `/mcp` manages MCP servers inside a session. `/mcp list` shows servers and their status, and `/mcp list-tools <server>` shows that server's tools. It uses the same configuration as `agent mcp`.

topics.title: MCP
topics.description: MCP (Model Context Protocol) connects Cursor to external tools and data sources such as issue trackers, databases and design tools. You configure servers in `.cursor/mcp.json` for a project or `~/.cursor/mcp.json` globally, using stdio, SSE or Streamable HTTP transports. Cursor asks for approval before running MCP tools, and remote servers can use OAuth.
resources: Cursor MCP — A 5-Minute Quick Start Guide
How to Use MCP Servers in Cursor

topics.title: @ Mentions
topics.description: Typing `@` in the chat input adds specific context to your prompt. You can mention files and folders, terminal output, previous chats, Git diffs such as your working state or branch, and the built-in browser. When you are not sure which files matter, you can skip mentions because the agent also searches by itself.
resources: @ Mentions in Cursor: Attaching Context to a Chat

topics.title: Mobile
topics.description: The Cursor app for iPhone and iPad lets you start agents on cloud machines or your own machines, follow them live and send follow-ups. You can review diffs and checks, merge pull requests, dictate or talk to the agent, and get notifications for running agents. It needs iOS or iPadOS 26.0 or later, and Android users can install the web app as a PWA.

topics.title: /model
topics.description: `/model` opens a list of models so you can switch without restarting. Add text to filter the list, and press `Tab` to edit the selection. The change applies to the current session.

topics.title: Models & Usage
topics.description: Models and usage cover which model runs your task and what it costs. You can pick a model, set its reasoning effort, let Auto choose for you, and use Cursor's own models or third-party ones. Paid plans include a pool of usage, and when it runs out you can wait for the reset, add credit or upgrade.

topics.title: models
topics.description: `agent models` lists the models available to your account. The `--list-models` flag does the same. Use a model ID from the list with `--model`.

topics.title: Parallel Cloud Agents
topics.description: Because each Cloud Agent has its own VM and branch, you can run many at the same time on different tasks. You can check on them from the Agents Window, the web, your phone, Slack, GitHub or Linear. Parallel runs are billed as usage at the model's rate, so watch your spend limit.
resources: Parallel AI Agents in Cursor 2.0: A Practical Guide

topics.title: Permissions & Safety
topics.description: Permissions and safety settings control what the agent can do without asking you. Run modes decide when an action needs approval, the terminal sandbox limits file and network access for shell commands, protections block risky actions even in automatic modes, and Privacy Mode keeps your code out of model training.

topics.title: Plan, Edit & Test
topics.description: For larger work, start in Plan Mode so the agent researches and proposes a plan before touching code. Then let it implement the plan, run your tests and fix failures. Splitting work into plan, edit and test steps keeps each change reviewable.
resources: The Best Cursor Feature | Cursor Plan Mode Explained

topics.title: /plan
topics.description: `/plan` switches the CLI to Plan mode, shows the current plan, or submits a prompt in Plan mode when you add text. The agent researches and proposes an approach before editing code. `Shift+Tab` also rotates between modes.

topics.title: Plan
topics.description: Plan Mode makes the agent research the code, ask clarifying questions and write an implementation plan before any code changes. You can edit the plan and then build it. Switch to it with `Shift+Tab`, or with `/plan` in the CLI. It works best for features that touch many files or have unclear requirements.
resources: How I Use Cursor Plan Mode for Real-World Feature Development
The Best Cursor Feature | Cursor Plan Mode Explained

topics.title: /plugin
topics.description: `/plugin` manages plugins and marketplaces from the CLI. Use it to install, list or remove plugins without opening the editor. Plugins can add skills, rules, MCP servers and hooks.

topics.title: Plugins
topics.description: Plugins bundle rules, skills, agents, commands, MCP servers and hooks into one package that you can share and install. You find them in the Cursor Marketplace, where official plugins are reviewed, or in a team marketplace set up by an admin. Install them from the Customize page at project or user scope.

topics.title: Project Instructions
topics.description: Project instructions are persistent guidance that Cursor places at the start of the model context. You write them as rules in `.cursor/rules` or as an `AGENTS.md` file, and you can add user rules for yourself and team rules for your organization. Use them for conventions the agent should follow every time, such as commands to run and code style.

topics.title: Queued Messages
topics.description: While the agent is working, pressing `Enter` queues your next message to run when the current task finishes. You can drag to reorder the queue, or use `Send now` to steer the agent at its next tool call. Queuing lets you keep giving instructions without interrupting work in progress.

topics.title: Reasoning Efforts
topics.description: Many models in Cursor come in variants with different reasoning effort, such as low, medium or high. Higher effort lets the model think longer, which can improve results on hard tasks but uses more tokens and takes more time. Fast is a separate option that speeds up responses at a higher price per token. The available levels and where you set them depend on the model and your Cursor version, and some plans fix them, for example Plus runs Cursor models at medium effort.

topics.title: /rename
topics.description: `/rename <name>` renames the current chat session. A clear name makes the chat easier to find later in `agent ls` or `/resume`. It is useful when you run several sessions on different tasks.

topics.title: /resume
topics.description: `/resume` opens a list of recent chats and resumes the one you choose. It works inside a running session, unlike `agent resume`, which you run from the shell. Your earlier context comes back with the chat.

topics.title: resume
topics.description: `agent resume` continues the latest chat session. If you need a specific one, use `agent --resume <chatId>`, and `--continue` is an alias for resuming the previous session. The restored conversation keeps its earlier context.

topics.title: Resuming
topics.description: Cursor keeps your past chats so you can return to them. In the CLI, `agent ls` lists previous chats, `agent resume` or `--continue` opens the latest one and `--resume <id>` loads a specific thread. Inside a session, `/resume` opens a list of recent chats. In the Agents Window, `Cmd+K` opens a palette that searches your past transcripts, and `Cmd+F` finds text inside an open conversation.

topics.title: Review Diffs
topics.description: Every agent edit appears as a diff, so you can read, accept, reject or ask for changes line by line. The Agents Window adds a diffs view where you can commit and manage pull requests. In the CLI, `Ctrl+R` opens a review of the changes.
resources: How You Can Automate Code Reviews in 3 Minutes with Cursor AI

topics.title: /rewind
topics.description: `/rewind` jumps back to an earlier message in the conversation. Use it when the agent went in a wrong direction and you want to continue from a previous point.

topics.title: rule
topics.description: `agent rule` (alias `agent generate-rule`) creates a Cursor rule through interactive prompts. The result is saved so the agent follows it in later sessions. Review the generated file before you commit it to the repository.

topics.title: Rules
topics.description: Rules are persistent instructions placed at the start of the model context. Project rules live in `.cursor/rules` as `.mdc` files with frontmatter that controls when they apply: always, when matching files are in context, when the agent decides they are relevant, or only when you mention them. Keep each rule short and focused, under about 500 lines.
resources: Cursor Rules: How They Work and When a Rule Beats a Skill
Cursor Rules guide for lazy devs. Setup rules in minutes with this quick tutorial!

topics.title: /run-everything
topics.description: `/run-everything [on|off|status]` toggles Run Everything or shows its state, and `/auto-run` is an alias. When it is on, the agent runs tool calls without asking. Turn it on only in environments where mistakes are cheap.

topics.title: Run Modes
topics.description: Run modes control when the agent can run actions without asking you. Auto-review lets allowlisted calls run, sends shell commands to a sandbox when possible and checks the rest with a classifier. Allowlist runs only approved actions, and Run Everything runs every tool call automatically with no sandbox. You choose the mode in Settings under Agents.

topics.title: /sandbox
topics.description: `/sandbox` configures sandbox mode and network access for commands the agent runs. It is the in-session version of the `--sandbox` flag. Settings persist between runs.

topics.title: Scaling Cursor
topics.description: Scaling Cursor means running more work at the same time without the tasks getting in each other's way. Git worktrees give each task its own checkout, subagents split work inside one task, and Cloud Agents run many tasks in parallel on their own machines.

topics.title: Sessions
topics.description: A session is a saved chat with the agent, including its context and history. Cursor keeps your past chats so you can come back to them. You can resume one, fork it into a new chat, rename it, rewind to an earlier message, and summarize a long conversation to free context.
resources: What are agent sessions? Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Grok
How to Carry Cursor Context Across Sessions (2026 Guide)

topics.title: Setting Up
topics.description: Setting up Cursor takes three steps. Install the desktop app, or the CLI if you work in a terminal, then sign in with your Cursor account and open a project folder. A one-click import can bring over your VS Code extensions, themes, settings and keybindings.

topics.title: /shell
topics.description: `/shell` enters Shell Mode, where you run quick non-interactive shell commands without leaving the conversation. `/sh` and `/run` are aliases. Commands are checked against your permissions, time out after 30 seconds and do not keep `cd` between commands.

topics.title: Shift+Tab
topics.description: `Shift+Tab` rotates between modes. In the editor chat input it switches to Plan Mode, and in the CLI it cycles through Agent, Plan and Ask. Use it to move from asking, to planning, to building.

topics.title: Side Chats
topics.description: A side chat is a full agent conversation linked to your main chat. It gets the main conversation as hidden reference context, but its own questions and answers stay out of the main thread. Open one with `/side` or `/btw`, or select text or a diff and choose "Ask in Side Chat". You can @-mention the side chat in the main thread to bring its findings back.
resources: Cursor Side Chats: Branch a Question Without Derailing

topics.title: Skills
topics.description: Skills are portable, version-controlled packages that teach the agent how to do a specific task. A skill is a folder with a `SKILL.md` file, with a `name` and `description` in frontmatter, and it can include scripts, references and assets. Skills live in `.cursor/skills/` or `.agents/skills/`, load on demand to save context, and can be called manually by typing `/` and choosing the skill.
resources: How to Create & Use SKILLS.md in Cursor

topics.title: status
topics.description: `agent status` shows whether you are logged in and which account is active. `agent whoami` is an alias, and `--format json` gives machine-readable output. Run it first if the CLI behaves as if you are signed out.

topics.title: Subagents
topics.description: Subagents are specialized assistants that the main agent delegates tasks to, each with its own context window. Built-in subagents such as Explore and Browser work automatically, and you can define custom ones as markdown files in `.cursor/agents/`. They can run in parallel or in the background, but each one uses its own tokens.
resources: Subagents: How They Work in Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and VS Code
Cursor Subagents: The Feature Everyone's Talking About

topics.title: Subscription Plans
topics.description: Cursor has individual plans for one person, plus Teams and Enterprise plans for organizations. Current individual plans are Free, Plus, Premium, Super and Ultra, with more included usage at each step. Cloud Agents, Automations, Bugbot, Auto and third-party models need Premium or higher, and older plans such as Pro and Pro+ keep working until you change them.
resources: Cursor Pricing in 2026: Every Plan, and Why Bills Surprise People

topics.title: /summarize
topics.description: `/summarize` condenses the conversation to reduce context use, and `/compress` is an alias. It helps when a long session starts to fill the context window. After summarizing, the agent keeps working with a shorter history.

topics.title: Tab
topics.description: In the editor, `Tab` accepts a Cursor Tab suggestion, and pressing it again jumps to the next predicted edit. In the CLI model picker, it edits the selected model. In the chat, the shortcuts page lists `Tab` as cycling to the next message.

topics.title: Terminal Sandbox
topics.description: The terminal sandbox runs agent shell commands with read and write access inside your workspace and with the network blocked by default. On macOS it uses Seatbelt, and on Linux it uses Landlock and seccomp. A command that needs more access runs outside the sandbox only after you approve it.

topics.title: Terminal Sandbox
topics.description: The terminal sandbox runs agent shell commands with read and write access inside your workspace and with the network blocked by default. On macOS it uses Seatbelt, and on Linux it uses Landlock and seccomp. A command that needs more access runs outside the sandbox only after you approve it.

topics.title: Third-Party Models
topics.description: Third-party models are models from providers such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Google that you can pick in Cursor next to its own models. They are not part of the weekly pool. On individual plans they need Premium or higher and are billed at the provider's API list price from prepaid credit, and on Teams and Enterprise a Cursor Token Rate applies to eligible models.
resources: Cursor First-Party vs Third-Party Usage Pools: 2026 Split Explained

topics.title: Usage Limits
topics.description: Current paid plans include one weekly pool of usage for Cursor models, shared across the editor, the CLI and Cloud Agents. Third-party models are not in the pool and draw on prepaid credit instead. When the pool runs out you can wait for the weekly reset, use prepaid credit or upgrade, and unused usage does not roll over. Older plans use two monthly pools plus optional on-demand usage.
resources: I Tested Usage Limits for Claude, Codex, and Cursor

topics.title: Using Cursor
topics.description: Once Cursor is installed, most daily work follows one loop. You describe a task, the agent searches and edits code, and you review the diff before you keep it. The rest is learning how to steer that loop: choosing an agent mode, giving the right context, managing sessions, and setting how much the agent can do without asking.
resources: Cursor Tutorial 2026: Beginner Guide to Agent in 15 Minutes
Cursor Crash Course for Beginners 2026 | Learn to Use Cursor FAST

topics.title: Voice Chat
topics.description: Voice chat is a realtime spoken conversation with an agent: you talk, it talks back, and you can hand it coding work without typing. You start it with the waveform button in the chat input when the input is empty. It works in the Agents Window, the editor, the web and the iOS app, and it is separate from dictation, which only turns speech into text.

topics.title: Ways to Use Cursor
topics.description: Cursor runs in several places, and they share the same agent, rules and MCP configuration. You can work in the desktop editor, in the Agents Window, from the terminal with Cursor CLI, in the cloud with Cloud Agents, and from the web or your phone. Cursor also connects to GitHub, Slack, Linear and Jira, and the Cursor SDK lets you call the agent from your own code.
resources: Unlocking Cursor: Features and Workflow Tips
Cursor Deep Dive: How Senior Engineers Actually Use Cursor for 10x Productivity

topics.title: Web
topics.description: Cursor Web at [cursor.com/agents](http://cursor.com/agents) lets you start and follow Cloud Agents from any browser. It also covers tasks the mobile app does not, such as the editor, terminal and file browser, environments and secrets, MCP server management, and rule and skill configuration. Agents started on the web also show up in the desktop app and on mobile.

topics.title: Web
topics.description: Cursor Web at cursor.com/agents lets you start and follow Cloud Agents from any browser. It also covers tasks the mobile app does not, such as the editor, terminal and file browser, environments and secrets, MCP server management, and rule and skill configuration. Agents started on the web also show up in the desktop app and on mobile.

topics.title: What is a Coding Agent?
topics.description: A coding agent is an AI system that completes programming tasks by taking actions, not just suggesting text. It can search many files, edit them, run shell commands, read the results and decide what to do next. Compared with autocomplete, you give it a goal and it carries out the steps while you supervise.
resources: What Are Coding Agents? A Developer's Guide to Agentic Coding (2026)

topics.title: What is Agentic Loop?
topics.description: An agentic loop is the cycle an agent repeats until a task is done. The model reasons over the current context, calls a tool such as searching files or running a command, observes the result and decides on the next step. In Cursor this loop is bounded by your run mode and approvals, so the agent pauses when it needs permission to go further.
resources: What Is an AI Agent Loop?
What Is Loop Engineering? Building Better AI Agents

topics.title: worker
topics.description: `agent worker` starts a private cloud worker that runs Cloud Agents on your own machine or infrastructure. This keeps code and execution in your environment. Options include labels, a pool mode for one agent at a time, and `--computer-use` to let agents control the desktop. `agent worker debug` runs preflight checks.

topics.title: /worktree
topics.description: `/worktree <task>` is an editor chat command that runs the rest of a chat in a separate Git checkout. You can commit and push from there, bring the changes back with `/apply-worktree` and remove the checkout with `/delete-worktree`. It keeps experimental work away from your main checkout. In the Agents Window, worktrees are built into the interface instead.

topics.title: Write Effective Prompts
topics.description: Good prompts state the outcome, name the relevant files and describe how to verify the result. Use `@` to point the agent at specific files or folders, and keep tasks small enough to review. If the result is wrong, make the prompt more specific and run it again instead of patching a long conversation.
resources: Best Cursor Prompts for Building Apps and Working With Codebases in 2026

topics.title: Your First Task
topics.description: A good first task is small and low risk. Open a project, open the agent with `Cmd+I` and ask it to explain the codebase, then ask for a few small improvements and pick one to implement. Review the changes in the diff view, then ask the agent to run your tests, type checks or build.
resources: Your First Project in Cursor: Open a Folder and Run Agent
Cursor 3 minute demo - the most popular AI code editor
